Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 1:

Surat al-Mulk (The Sovereignty)

It is also called Tabarak (Blessed), al-Mani'a (The Preventer), al-Munjiya (The Saviour) and al-Mujadila (The Pleader). Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "In the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), we used to call it al-Mani'a."

At-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "One of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) pitched his tent over a grave, without realising it was a grave. It turned out to be the grave of a man who was reciting Surat al-Mulk until he finished it. So he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him. The Messenger of Allah, upon him be prayer and peace, said: 'It is al-Mani'a, it is al-Munjiya; it saves its reciter from the punishment of the grave.'"

Al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and 'Abd ibn Humayd in his Musnad, with the wording being his, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said to a man: "Shall I present you with a hadith that will delight you?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Recite: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the sovereignty﴾ [al-Mulk: 1], and teach it to your family, all your children, the young ones of your household and your neighbours. For it is al-Munjiya and al-Mujadila on the Day of Resurrection before its Lord, for its reciter, and it seeks for him that He save him from the punishment of the Fire, and its companion is saved by it from the punishment of the grave." The report ends.

In Jamal al-Qurra' it is also called al-Waqiya (The Protector) and al-Mannaa'a (The Withholder). It is Meccan according to the more correct view. It was said that it is Meccan except for three verses of it, and Ibn Juwayr narrated in his tafsir from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. In a strange view it is Medinan. Its verses number thirty in the Meccan and the last Medinan, and thirty in the rest; what favours this will come shortly, God willing.

The connection of this surah with what precedes it is that when God, exalted is He, set forth a parable for the disbelievers in the two women, both destined for wretchedness, even though they were under two great prophets, and a parable for the believers in Asiya and Maryam, both destined for happiness, even though most of their people were disbelievers, He opened this surah with what indicates His all-encompassing power, His domination, and His disposal of His dominion according to what His decree has preceded.

Another view: the beginning of this surah is connected to His saying at the end of Surat al-Talaq: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens﴾ [al-Talaq: 12], because it contains greater elaboration of what relates to that. It was separated by Surat al-Tahrim, since it is like a piece of Surat al-Talaq and its completion. Many reports have come concerning its virtues, among them what has already passed, and among them what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and others narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, a surah in the Book of Allah, which has only thirty verses, interceded for a man until he was forgiven: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the sovereignty﴾."

Among them is what came in a hadith narrated by al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh with a good chain from Ibn Mas'ud, and another narrated from him by a group, and authenticated by al-Hakim: "Whoever recites it in a night has earned much and good."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'isha that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite Alif Lam Mim Tanzil (al-Sajda) and Blessed is He in whose hand is the sovereignty every night; he would not leave them, whether on a journey or at home."

For this and similar reports, it was said that reciting it every night is recommended. Praise be to Allah who has granted me success in reciting it thus from the time I reached the age of discernment until today, and I ask Allah, exalted is He, for success in what follows and for acceptance. I have seen in some commentaries on Sahih al-Bukhari the recommendation of reciting it upon sighting the crescent, hoping for protection from what is disliked in that month, by the blessing of its thirty verses. And Allah, exalted is He, is the Granter of success.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the sovereignty﴾. Barakah (blessing) is growth and increase, whether sensory or intellectual, and abundance of good and its permanence. Its attribution to Allah, mighty and majestic, according to the first meaning, which is the most fitting to the context, is in consideration of His exaltedness, mighty and majestic, above all else in His essence, attributes and acts. The form tafa'ala (tabaraka) is for intensification in this, as in its counterparts among forms that cannot be conceived as attributed to Him, exalted is He, such as takabbara (to be proud). According to the second meaning, in consideration of the abundance of what overflows from Him, glorified is He, upon His creatures of all kinds of good. The form then may be for indicating the growth of those goods and their increase little by little and moment by moment, according to their occurrence or the occurrence of what relates to them. It was said: since it independently indicates the utmost perfection and announces the extreme of magnification, it is not permissible to use it of other than Him, glorified is He, nor to use other forms of it of Him, blessed and exalted is He. The complete discussion of this point has passed. Its attribution to the relative pronoun serves to cite what is in the relative clause as evidence for the realisation of its content, because what is meant is that He, glorified is He, is of complete encompassing and dominion, on the basis that "in whose hand is the sovereignty" is a metaphorical representational metaphor for that, and it is not permissible in any of its individual terms; or that sovereignty is in its literal sense and the hand is a metaphor for encompassing and dominion, as has been said. Such dominion requires that the one characterised by it is self-sufficient while others are dependent on him for their existence and for the perfections of their existence, so he has exclusive ownership of what exists. Likewise, in common usage, "sovereignty" is not applied to what is not like this. Therefore it was said here, explaining the meaning of the verse: exalted and magnified in His essence above all else in essence, attribute and act, is the one of complete encompassing and dominion over every existing thing.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and He is over all things Powerful﴾ completes this, because the first clause indicates complete disposal of existents according to the requirement of His will and volition, without any disputant or opposer, and no one disposes of them but Him, mighty and majestic, as the fronting of the adverbial phrase indicates. The second indicates complete and comprehensive power. Had it been limited to the first, it would have suggested that His disposal, exalted is He, is restricted to changing the conditions of a king, as is seen in the figurative disposal of kings. Therefore it was joined with the second, to indicate that He, mighty is His authority, is capable of disposal, of bringing into existence the entities disposed of, and of bringing into existence their essential and other accidents. For this reason, it is followed by the attribute that includes accidents. This is what al-'Allama al-Tibi preferred. The author of al-Kashshaf preferred, for the first clause, what we mentioned of restricting it to existents, and said: that is, exalted and magnified above the attributes of created beings, He in whose hand is the sovereignty over every existent, for what you have heard. And for the second, he restricted it to the non-existent, and said: and He is over everything not yet existing that falls under power, Powerful. Its rationale, according to what is in al-Kashf, is that "thing" (shay') though general to everything that may be known and spoken of, when joined with power is restricted to the non-existent, since the existent is independent of an agent according to the majority of theologians who hold that the cause of need is createdness, and this is the view of al-Zamakhshari and his followers.

As for those who hold that the cause of need is contingency, like the verifiers, the reason is that choice requires the prior non-existence. The second clause was brought for this too, for completion, because restricting it to the existent implies a deficiency. The author of al-Taqrib preferred that His saying, ﴿in whose hand is the sovereignty﴾, is unrestricted, and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and He is over all things Powerful﴾ is general to what the word "thing" is applied to. Thus he intends to state power first and its generality second. The procedure of al-Zamakhshari was not accepted, and it was objected to that "thing" either is restricted to the existent or includes both existent and non-existent; on either view there is no reason to restrict it to what has not existed when each is added to it. Except that it may be said he restricted it to differ from what precedes it, since he restricted the first to the existent. There is also a problem with this: if the second were general, the difference would still be realised, yet the hand is a metaphor for power; if it is restricted to power, as is his view, the first is restricted to the non-existent; and if it is not restricted, the second is not restricted to the non-existent. The author of al-Kashf claimed its falling was established by what we quoted from him, and it was objected to and answered with something not free of consideration, so let it be considered.

Some people took "sovereignty" to mean the existents, and made "in whose hand" a metaphor for power, so the meaning would be "in His existing power." One of them objected that there is weakness in this, and indicated that its escape is either by making the hand a metaphor for disposal, or by explaining sovereignty as disposal. It was said that what is meant by sovereignty being in His hand, exalted is He, is that He, mighty and majestic, is its owner, so the meaning of "in whose hand is the sovereignty" is the owner of sovereignty. Al-Raghib explained "sovereignty" in such contexts as the controlling of a thing disposed of by judgement, and its restriction to the world of witnessing became common, and the counterpart in that case would be malakut (the unseen dominion), but that is not what is meant here, as is not hidden.

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿He who created death and life﴾, begin an explanation of some of the rulings of sovereignty and the effects of power, and a clarification that they are founded upon the laws of wisdom and interests and that they lead to sublime ends. The relative pronoun (al-ladhi) is a substitute (badal) for the first relative pronoun, and its relative clause is like the first in bearing witness to His exaltedness, Mighty and Majestic is He. Al-Tabarsi (d. 548 AH) permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is the One who..." etc.

Death, according to the view of many of the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), is an existential attribute that is opposite to life. They used as evidence for its existence that creation is connected to it, and creation is not connected to a non-existent thing, because the annihilation of things is eternal.

As for what has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, that Allah the Exalted created death in the form of a white-spotted black ram that passes by nothing without it dying, and created life in the form of a dappled mare that passes by nothing, and nothing smells its fragrance without coming to life, this is most like the speech of the Sufis, whose apparent meaning cannot be understood. It has also been said that it is given in the manner of imagery and depiction. The Qadariyyah (Qadariyyah, a sect that affirms human free will) and some of the people of the Sunnah held that death is a negative matter, namely the absence of life from that which should have life, and this is the most immediate and closest meaning. The argument from the verse was answered by saying that "creation" in it means "measuring/decreeing," and this is connected to a negative matter just as it is connected to an existent one; or that ﴿death﴾ is not absolute pure non-existence but rather the non-existence of a specific thing, and creation and bringing into being may be connected to such a thing, on the basis that it is the giving of existence to another even if not giving existence to the thing itself; or that creation means origination and establishing, not bringing into being, and in this sense it applies to negative matters; or that the statement has an implied genitive construction, meaning "He created the causes of death"; or that what is meant by the creation of ﴿death and life﴾ is the creation of a time and a specific duration for them, which none knows except Allah the Exalted, so their bringing into being is a figurative expression for bringing into being their time. The state of these possibilities is not hidden.

Among the strange views is what has been said: that by death He meant the world, since death occurs in it, and by life He meant the Hereafter, since there is no death in it; so it is as if it were said: "He who created the world and the Hereafter." The truth, however, is that both are in their real meaning. Death is as you have heard, and life is an existential attribute without disagreement; it is that by whose existence perception is valid, or a meaning added to knowledge and power which brings about for the one characterized by it a state that did not exist before, of the validity of knowledge and power. Placing death before life, if death is taken as absolute non-existence, namely the absence of life from that which should have it, is evident, because it precedes existence. If death is taken as the subsequent non-existence, as is most suitable to the purpose here, namely the absence of life from one who was characterized by it, there is great admonition, reminder and restraint from committing sins, and an incitement to good action. For this reason it was reported: "Increase your remembrance of the destroyer of pleasures," (the Prophet ﷺ said it).

Even if they [i.e., life and its benefits] call to that, since whoever knows that it is a great blessing and is a person of insight acts to thank Allah the Exalted for it, yet it is not equal to death in that respect. Whoever claims that there is no call in it at all, and that it is mentioned only in respect of action depending upon it, has not examined the matter carefully.

The definite article (al-) in both places is a replacement for the genitive construct, meaning: "He who created your passing death and your life, O you who are responsible (mukallafun)." ﴿That He may test you﴾, i.e., that He may deal with you as one who tests you; ﴿which of you is best in deed﴾, i.e., most correct and most sincere, so He will reward you according to graded ranks corresponding to the gradations of your deeds. The root meaning of trial (balaʾ) is testing, and because it implies lack of knowledge of what is tested, which is not valid with regard to Him Mighty and Majestic, interpreting the statement as mentioned leads to the figurative metaphorical expression (istiʿarah tamthiliyyah), and considering a subordinate metaphor (istiʿarah tabiʿiyyah) in it instead of it is inferior in eloquence. What is meant by deed includes the deed of the heart and the deed of the limbs; for this reason the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the verse: "Which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah the Exalted, and quickest in obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

That is: which of you is most complete in understanding what proceeds from the presence of Allah the Exalted, and most perfect in preserving what is taken from His address, glorified is He. The use of the comparative form, although the trial includes the responsible persons according to their deeds, which are divided into good and bad and not merely good and better, is to signal that the essential purpose and principal aim of the trial is the manifestation of the perfection of the goodness of the good-doers, while the basic faith and obedience are realized also in the rest, because the causes for it are fully mutually supporting. As for turning away from this, it is far from being included in it, let alone being part of the aim or the presumed purpose according to those who consider the acts of Allah Mighty and Majestic to have aims; rather, it is an action that proceeds from its doer due to his poor choice, without any justification for it or closeness to it. In it there is an incitement to ascend to the heights of knowledge and the stages of acts of obedience, and a restraint from engaging in their deficiencies, which is not hidden.

Some have made this a case of absolute addition, or of the type of ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station?﴾ [Maryam: 73], "is not that (the case)." ("Which of you is best in deed?") is a subject and predicate, and the clause is in the place of accusative as a second object of ﴿that He may test you﴾, according to what is in the Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari), because it includes the meaning of knowledge. Is this kind called suspension (taʿlīq) or not? It is said there is disagreement about it. In al-Bahr (of Abu Hayyan), on the authority of his companions, it is said that it is called that. He said: when the verb is transitive to two objects and the first is put in the accusative and it is followed by an interrogative clause or a clause introduced by the particle of the beginning (lam al-ibtidaʾ) or a negative particle, the clause is said to suspend the verb, and it is in the position of the accusative as if it had occurred in the position of the two objects; and in it is something that suspends the verb from action. In the Kashshaf, here it is not called suspension; suspension is only that one places after the verb that is suspended something that fills the place of both objects together, such as your saying: "I know which of them is Zayd" and "I know whether Zayd is departing," but when one of the two objects is mentioned after it, such as "I know the people, which of them is most excellent," this is not suspension.

The verse is of this kind. It was objected to by the author of al-Taqrib that the knowing is implicit, and it is the suspending element, as said by al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj, and it does not necessarily follow that the object is mentioned with it; rather the estimate is "that He may test you, so that He may know which of you is best." Also, an interrogative clause does not occur as a second object of "I knew," but rather it occupies the place of the two objects in "I knew which of them went out," because the meaning is "I knew the answer to this question," and there is no sense in estimating the like in "I knew it, which of them went out." It was answered that implication dispenses with the need for implicit supposition, and that the interrogative clause not occurring as a second object is weak, because when it occurs as a first object, as in ﴿We will surely drag out from every faction whichever of them is most rebellious﴾ [Maryam: 69], in the sense of "We will drag out those of whom it is said 'which of them is most...'," as al-Khalil said, then its occurrence as a second object is not impossible, by interpreting it as "that He may make you know those about whom it is said ﴿which of them is best﴾." This was the view of al-Tibi. Then he said: The author of al-Intisaf has been fair when he said: suspension from one of the two objects is subject to disagreement, and the more correct view is the one chosen by al-Zamakhshari; and this kind is its nest, in which it creeps and knows how to enter and exit, end of quote.

What he mentioned in Surah Hud is that in the verse there is suspension, because testing includes the meaning of knowing, since it is a path to it, and he gave as an example "look which of them is best in face" [cf. Hud: 7]. They took his two statements to be contradictory. In al-Kashf, his statement there clearly states that the suspension in it is in the sense of suspending a heart verb when followed by an interrogative; and in this sense it is specific to the heart verb without restriction to the seven that take two objects. The exception to interrogatives only, not to what contains the particle of beginning or the like, was explicitly stated by Shaykh Ibn al-Hajib in a text. So it does not contradict what he mentioned in this surah, that it is not suspension; the negation of suspension is only in the well-known sense.

[Page 5]

As for taking it as implicit in the verse of Hud and implication in the verse of the Kingdom for variety, there is no justification for it after his explicit statement that it is a metaphor. This, too, according to this, has no justification for the one there being a choice of the view of al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj, while the one here is a choice of another view. So reflect and take heed, for this is often asked about, in former and recent times. And Allah the Exalted is the Granter of success.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, i.e., the Overpowering, whom the punishment of the one who did evil cannot frustrate; ﴿the Forgiving﴾ toward whomever He wills of them, or toward whoever repents, according to what some of them chose, because it is more suitable to the context.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 67, verse 3:

﴿Who created seven heavens﴾. It has been said that this is an adjective (*na't*) for "the Mighty, the Forgiving," or an explicative apposition (*bayan*), or a substitute (*badal*).

Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) preferred that it is in the accusative or nominative case, in the mode of praise (*al-madh*), and that it is connected in meaning to the two preceding relative clauses (*al-mawsulayn*), even though grammatically it is detached from them. It is joined with them in the string of testimony to His teachings, may He be glorified and exalted, and with the second relative clause in being a source of trial, as expressed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was on the water, that He may test you [as to] which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud: 7].

His saying, ﴿*tibaqan*﴾ [in layers], is an adjective of *sab'* (seven). That the adjective belongs to the genitive noun (the number) is not obligatory, but rather the more common usage. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) from *taabaqtu al-na'l bil-na'l* (I fitted one sandal to the other) when you stitch them together. It is described by it for emphasis, or by omitting a modified noun, meaning "possessors of layers," or by interpreting it as an active participle (*ism al-maf'ul*), meaning "fitted/matched."

It is permitted that it be an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) emphasizing a deleted verb, meaning "they were fitted in layers," and the sentence is then in the place of an adjective. It is also permitted that it be the plural of *tabaq*, like *jamal* and *jimal*, or the plural of *tabaqah*, like *rahbah* (with the *ha'* vowelled with a fatha) and *rihab*. In that case the statement contains an implied genitive construction, since it is a solid noun that is not described by an adjective; the meaning is "possessors of layers." It has also been said that it may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from ﴿seven heavens﴾, due to its proximity to the definite, by virtue of its encompassing all of them and there being no single one beyond that. This was refuted by the argument that, after all the discussion, the most it amounts to is something like "the sun," which is restricted to one unique item, and a later circumstantial clause cannot come from such a thing; thus one does not say "a shining sun rose over us."

In any case, the meaning, as ʿAbd ibn Humayd recorded, is that some of them are above others. There is no proof in this for their being pressed tightly together, as the early philosophers and those Muslims who agreed with them claimed, contrary to what the authentic hadiths report. Yet I do not think that one who denies this is an unbeliever.

They differed about their materials. It was said: the first is of a sea-like substance that is held back (*mawj makfuf*), the second of white pearl, the third of iron, the fourth of copper, the fifth of silver, the sixth of gold, and the seventh of white emerald. Other things have been said, and I do not think you will find a report that can be relied upon concerning what has been said, even if you flew to the heaven. I think that if you did find one, you would have interpreted it figuratively, while maintaining the belief that God, Mighty and Majestic, is powerful over all things.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿what you see in the creation of the Most Merciful of any inconsistency﴾, is another adjective for the seven heavens, according to al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari). In it he placed ﴿the creation of the Most Merciful﴾ in the position of the connecting pronoun, for the sake of exalting [the subject] and for indicating the reason for the ruling, such that a syllogism of the first figure may be formed which yields the negation of seeing any inconsistency in them. [It also serves] to show that He, Mighty and Majestic, created them by His overpowering might out of mercy and bounty, and that in their creation there are magnificent blessings.

What Ibn Hisham mentioned in the fourth chapter of *al-Mughni*, that a descriptive clause is connected only by a pronoun, either stated or implied, is not a proof against Jar Allah. The reconciliation that this applies when the speaker does not intend exaltation is not valid, because there must be a rhetorical purpose (*nukta*), whether it is exaltation or something else.

Abu Hayyan favored that it is a resumptive new sentence (*isti'naf*), and that the creation of the Most Merciful is general, covering the heavens and other things, and that the address is to everyone who is fit to be addressed. It was permitted that it be addressed to the master of those addressed, ﷺ. But the first seems preferable. The *min* in ﴿*min*﴾ is for emphasizing negation, meaning "you see nothing," ﴿of any inconsistency﴾, i.e., discord and lack of proportion, as Qatadah and others said, from *al-fawt* (failure), since each of two mismatched things lacks some of what is in the other. Some interpreted *tafawut* as a thing exceeding the limit it should have, either by excess or deficiency, and this is what is meant by discord. On this is the saying of one of the men of letters:

*Its limbs are proportioned, so you see no discord in them, but rather they come in measure.*

Al-Suddi said: that is, of any defect, and to this returns the view of the one who said: that is, of any inconsistency that causes deficiency. ʿAta ibn Yasar said:

[Page 7]

That is, of non-uniformity. It was said: that is, of disturbance. It was said: that is, of crookedness. It was said: that is, of contradiction. All of these return to what we have mentioned. Among the strange views is what was said by the shaykh of the unveiling sect (*al-Taifa al-Kashfiyya*) in our time: that among all things there is a connection, a kind of mutual attraction, by which none of them fails from another. Interpreting the verse in this way, and in this direction, is the view of the philosophers today, who claim that among bodies, both the higher and the lower, there is mutual attraction at specific measures, by which their positions are preserved and some are bound to others. However, some of them held that what causes the attraction and connection weakens little by little, in a way that its effect does not appear except over very long periods.

From this they inferred that this observed world must necessarily depart from this sensible order, so that collisions and the like occur among bodies. They said: if this is the Resurrection, then so be it. The condition of what he said and what they said is not hidden, and the verse, as has been heard, is far removed from all of that.

ʿAbd Allah (ibn Mas'ud), ʿAlqamah, al-Aswad, Ibn Jubayr, Talhah and al-Aʿmash read ﴿*min tafawwut*﴾ with a shadda on the waw, the verbal noun of *tafawwata*. Abu Zayd related from the Arabs ﴿*fi tafawut*﴾ with fatha, damma and kasra on the waw, and the fatha and kasra are both anomalous (*shadhdhan*), as in *al-Bahr* (of Abu Hayyan).

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So return the gaze; do you see any rifts?﴾ is connected to what precedes it in the sense of causation, meaning: because of the report of that. For it is a cause for the command to look again, to repel what might be suspected of doubt. So in meaning it is the answer to an implied condition: meaning, if you are in doubt about that, then return your gaze until the matter becomes clear and no doubt or suspicion remains for you about the realization of what that statement contained of the proportion of the creation of the Most Merciful and its possession of what befits Him.

*Al-Futur* (rifts): Mujahid said: the cracks, the plural of *fatr*, which is a split; it is said: he split it, and it split apart (*fataraho fa-infatar*). The apparent meaning is a split in general, not specifically a lengthwise split, though that is its original sense, as al-Raghib said. In the same sense is Abu ʿUbaydah's saying: the fissures. They recited the verse of ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿUqbah ibn Masʿud:

*You split the heart, then you scattered into it your love, so it was cut open, and the rift was mended.*

And al-Suddi said: the breaches. All of this is intended, as is understood from the words of some of the eminent scholars, to mean a flaw. Qatadah explained it so, and Ibn ʿAbbas explained it as weakness.

The clause ﴿do you see﴾ etc. Abu Hayyan said: it is in the place of an accusative object for a deleted verb that is suspended, meaning: so look, do you see? Or, within ﴿return the gaze﴾ there is the meaning of "so look with your eye."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 4:

﴿Then return your gaze twice﴾. That is, two more returns in searching for a flaw. The dual here is meant as repetition and multiplicity, as they say in "labbayka" and "sa'dayka" (meaning: repeated responses to You, again and again). That is, return the gaze again and again, many returns one after another. This is just as the dual in the original form (al-muthanna) is intended to express multiplicity in the verse:

"For the promise of a grave, and a grave was the most honoured of them in dwelling and the furthest of them from the abode of the reproacher."

What is meant is: if you were to return to many graves. It has also been said that the dual is to be taken literally, and that he was commanded to return his gaze to the sky twice, since an error may occur in the first look, so he corrects it with the second; or the first is to see its beauty and evenness, and the second is to observe its stars in their course and their end. But this is not correct. The first view is supported by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Your gaze will return to you humbled (khasi'an)﴾, for it is the answer to the command, and an answer implies a necessary consequence, and what it contains does not generally follow from the two looks. The meaning is: the gaze will return to you deprived of finding what it sought of flaw or defect, as if it had been driven away in humiliation, based on what is said: that it is derived from "khasa'a al-kalb" (the dog was driven off), i.e., he drove it away, taken as a metaphor. However, in al-Sihah it is said: "khasa'a basarahu khasan wa khas'aan," meaning he dazzled, and dazzlement confuses the sight. So interpreting ﴿khasi'an﴾ as (bewildered) is closer to taking it from that sense.

It seems they preferred the preceding view because it contains clear exaggeration and eloquence, and it is further removed from repetition in its outcome, together with His words ﴿and it will be weary (haseer)﴾, that is, exhausted from long repetition and frequent re-examination. It is said: "hasira ba'iruhu yahsaru husuran," meaning (became exhausted) and worn out, so he is haseer and mahsur. Al-Raghib said: al-hasr is the uncovering of what clothes something from what is upon it; one says "hasarat 'an al-dhira'" (she uncovered the forearm). The haseer is one who has no armour or helmet. A she-camel that is haseer is one from which flesh and strength have been stripped, and the plural is husr. Also, al-hasir means one whose strengths have been exposed; he is also called mahsur. The haseer is one imagined to have stripped his own strength, while the mahsur is one imagined to have been stripped by fatigue. In the verse, haseer may mean either haasir or mahsur, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), like the preceding description of the gaze. It may also be a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun within it. Al-Kharazmi, reading from al-Kisa'i, recited "yanqalibu" in the nominative (raf'), and it was interpreted as a clause in the position of a hal that is presumed (hal muqaddara).

[Page 8]

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And We have certainly adorned the heaven﴾ and so on, is a statement intended to urge reflection upon [God's] power and to remind of [His] favor. In the Irshad (*Irshad al-Aql al-Salim*, by Abu al-Su'ud) there is an explanation that the creation of the heavens is in the utmost beauty and splendor, following the explanation of their being free (*khuluww*) from any blemish or deficiency. The sentence is introduced with an oath to show the utmost concern with its content, meaning: "And by God, We have certainly adorned the heaven ﴿of this world﴾ [that is nearest] to you," i.e., the one that is closest to you of the others. Its nearness is in relation to what is beneath it, but in relation to those around the Throne, it is the reverse. ﴿with lamps﴾: the plural of *misbah*, which is a lamp (*siraj*). It has been used figuratively for a star, and then the word was made plural; or lamps were used figuratively from the beginning for stars. Some lexicographers explained it as "the place where the lamp is kept," in which case it becomes a figurative usage upon a figurative usage, and there is no need for it, given their explicit statement that *misbah* is itself also the lamp. Its being indefinite is for magnification, meaning: "with great lamps, unlike your lamps which you know." It has been said that it is for variety, but the first is preferable.

The apparent meaning is that what is intended is the stars that shine at night with the light of a lamp, from among the wandering planets and the fixed stars, based on the view that they are all in orbits and courses that vary in nearness and distance, within the thickness of the lowest heaven. That the heaven is the orbit (*falak*) is contrary to what is known from the salaf (the early generations), and it is only a view held by one who wished to reconcile the statements of the early philosophers with the statements of the Sharia, and it spread among the Muslims, and whoever believed it believed it. From 'Ata' it is reported that the stars are in lamps suspended between the heaven and the earth by chains of light in the hands of angels; and upon this, ﴿We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾ is like the saying of the speaker:

*"I adorned the ceiling with lamps."*

This is clear, but the report hardly can be considered sound. As for whoever believes that the lowest heaven is the orbit of the moon, and the remaining six are the orbits of the remaining planets in the well-known order, and that the fixed stars have a special orbit called in the language of the Sharia the Kursi (Footstool), or it is allowed that these [stars] are in the orbit of Saturn, which is the seventh heaven, or that some of them are in one orbit and some of them in another above it, or that each of them is in an orbit and a heaven other than the seven: restricting [the count] to a small number does not negate a large one. [The one who says this] stated: The specification of the heaven for the adornment with them is because they are only seen upon it, and the body of what is above it is not seen; or in consideration of what the understanding of the common people requires, since it is impossible for them to distinguish between one heaven and another. So they see the stars as glittering jewels upon the carpet of the nearer blue sphere. And whoever considers what the people of astronomy (*hay'a*) hold today, that the stars are wonders of divine power, floating in the sea of the atmosphere of space in a particular manner required by wisdom, and their courses in it are their orbits, and they have moved, as they have moved, in emptiness or something similar, with forces by which they attract one another and are bound together, and they have motions on their own axes and motions other than that, and they are not fixed as is well known in solid transparent bodies, neither heavy nor light, called orbits or heavens, and they vary in nearness and distance with a total variation, even though they all appear near due to a cause still hidden from them—so that some of them do not reach us with their light except after several years, although the light of the sun and between us and it is thirty-four million farsakhs, and a million is a thousand thousand, reaching us in eight minutes and thirteen seconds—and so on with what they claim about them.

He said: It is permissible that by the lowest heaven is meant a specific layer in this space, and by the lamps are stars in it itself, which have adorned that layer with them in the way that the space of a house is adorned by birds that fly and hover in it, for example; or [the lamps are] all of the stars that are seen, even if they are above it, and their adornment is by their manifestation in it, as has passed. You know that whoever undertakes to apply the verses and reports to what the philosophers said absolutely has undertaken a matter that hardly can be completed for him; and God and His Messenger (ﷺ) have more right to be followed. Indeed, the interpretation of the transmitted text is only appropriate when a rational proof stands against what it indicates; and most of the proofs of the philosophers are a foundation for incapacity to establish them with sound establishment, and they contradict the proofs of the people of the Sharia, as is not hidden from whoever has been illuminated by their lamps.

﴿and We have made them missiles against the devils﴾: the pronoun refers to the lamps according to what is apparent, not to the lowest heaven, in the sense of "We made from them," i.e., from its direction, as it has been said. The *rujum* (missiles) is the plural of *rajm* (with a fatha), which is a verbal noun that has been applied to what is thrown, i.e., hurled; so it has the rule of solid nouns, and for this reason it is pluralized, although the original rule for verbal nouns is that they are not pluralized. It has been said that here it is a verbal noun in the sense of *rajm* (hurling) as well. What is meant by the devils are those who eavesdrop (*mustaraqu al-sam'*), and their being hurled, according to what is well known, is by the streaking down of meteors caused by the stars; and many of the commentators went to this, and it is based on what the earlier philosophers established, that the stars themselves do not streak down, but what streaks down are fiery flames arising from particles rising to the sphere of fire; but through the stars' heating of the earth [these are caused], so the figurative usage is either in the attribution of the making to them or in the word itself, and it is a metaphor through intermediaries.

Al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) said: There is no obstacle to the streaking body itself being of the kind of the stars, even if this contradicts the belief of the philosophers and astronomers; but in the divine texts there is what indicates that they are missiles against the devils, end quote. I say: it is not hidden that this foundation also is not complete except by the establishment of the sphere of fire, which you will not see them establish except by the occurrence of these meteors; and the early community (*salaf*) do not say this, nor do the people of the new philosophy; and these have not yet verified the matter of these meteors, but they incline to the view that they are bodies that separated from the stars they claim, worlds containing mountains and the like, as the earth contains such; and for some events they went out of the limit of the attractive forces of those [stars] toward what they were separated from, and did not reach the limit where the force of the earth attracts them; so they remain revolving at the boundary of the earth's sphere and the air surrounding it; so when it happens that they enter the air of the earth during their motion, they burn, wholly or partly, just as some bodies protected from air burn when the air strikes them; and perhaps in some of their motions they reach the limit of the earth's attraction and so fall upon it.

Some of them claim about the stones falling from the atmosphere, which they call among themselves *aerolites* (meaning air-stones), that they are from those bodies; and all of that is a tale of superstition and a hurling by corrupt conjectures. The most that can be said about these meteors is that they may be arising from bodies of the kind of the stars in which there is the power of burning, whether every luminous thing is burning or not, formed in the atmosphere of this observable space; but because of their extreme smallness they are not seen even with telescopes until, when brought near by their streaking down, they are seen. And they may encounter, in their streaking down, bodies rising from the earth and burn them; and perhaps the burning reaches what is very near the earth, and perhaps stones are formed from that.

Then the intellect allows that they may have a revolution in some shape, so they return after what is seen of their streaking down, and that they may vanish after their streaking down, and God, the Exalted, creates others from a substance that none knows but He, Mighty and Majestic.

The pronoun in the accusative in (*ja'alnaha*, "We made them") although it refers to the lamps, yet it refers to them only in consideration of the kind, not the specific quality of their being the adornment of the lowest heaven, like ﴿And none is granted a lengthening of life, nor is anything reduced from his lifespan﴾ (Fatir 35:11); and my dirham and its half [idiom]. Because the adornment is with consideration of visibility, and these bodies have no visibility before their streaking down; and if it is considered in their being lamps or stars or planets, their visibility in themselves is considered, and to those near them, without the specificity of their visibility to us. And in their being an adornment for the heaven, [is their being an adornment for it] in general; so the matter is very clear.

It is possible that they arise from the visible lamps, with which [the heaven] is adorned, by their separating from them while they are in their place as flames, which are the meteors; and that is only like a brand taken from a fire, while the fire remains fixed. This was the view of al-Jubba'i (Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i) and many others. And it is plausible, because each of them may have the capacity to separate off that, and the capacity may belong to some of them and not others. And this [is said] because of lack of knowledge of the realities of the heavenly bodies and their states in themselves. The discourse is like your saying: "The emir settled the tribe of such-and-such in the frontier of such-and-such and made them shoot with muskets whoever came near it"; for it does not follow that each one of them has the capacity to shoot. Then it does not follow that every meteor seen is a brand from the lamps; rather, it is permissible that some of it—namely that with which the devils are pelted from them—and some of it from matters that occur in the atmosphere, such as friction or the like.

The variation of the meteors in fewness and abundance may be due to variation in atmospheric events, or to variation in eavesdropping. There is no text in the verses and reports stating explicitly that meteors occur only for the pelting of the devils; so it is possible that most meteors are from atmospheric events, and the tailed ones among them—in the view of the earlier scholars—and in themselves, apart from their tails, are very numerous stars that revolve, not as other stars revolve, so that they come near at times and go far at others, leaving the orbits of the planets for places where they are not seen at all according to the philosophers of this age; and they have a discourse about them longer than their tails. And Imam al-Razi raised in this section questions and doubts, which he answered as he answered; and we have done something similar in what preceded, in a more complete manner; so let it be remembered.

We have elaborated there at length on what relates to this station; but some of what we mentioned there—take from both places what is pure and leave what is turbid, after you reflect with the utmost reflection and contemplate. It has been said: the meaning of the verse is "We made them conjectures and missiles by the unseen for the devils of mankind," namely the astrologers, who believe in the influence of the stars on happiness, misery, and the like. We have refuted them, i.e., the refutation was in what preceded; so return to it if you wish, for it is very precious.

﴿And We have prepared for them﴾, i.e., We made ready for the devils, ﴿the punishment of the blaze﴾, the punishment of the kindled, blazing fire in the Hereafter, after burning in this world with meteors. And that they were created from fire does not prevent this, for they are not fire alone, but it is their predominant element; so it is from them like dust from the children of Adam, and thus they are affected by it; besides, it will be a fire stronger than fire. The verse has been used as evidence that the fire is created now, and that the devils are accountable.

[Page 9]

﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord﴾ [the phrase is understood as] apart from the devils, or including them and others, on the basis that this is a generalization after a specification, in order to remove the suspicion that the punishment is restricted to them. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur) is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and His statement, ﴿the punishment of Hell﴾, is the postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). The restriction (al-hasr) is relative (idafi), by virtue of the indicative texts that refer to the punishment of the disobedient. So there is no proof in it for those among the Murji'ah (a theological school that held that only unbelievers are punished) who say: "None but the disbelievers are punished."

al-Dahhak, al-A'raj, Usayd ibn Usayd al-Muzani and Hasan, in the narration of Harun from him, read "ʿadhaba" (the punishment) in the accusative case, as a conjunction with ﴿the punishment of the Blaze﴾ (from the previous verse). That is: "And We have prepared for those who disbelieve the punishment of Hell." ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾, i.e., Hell.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 7:

﴿When they are cast into it﴾, i.e., they are thrown into it as firewood is thrown into a great fire, ﴿they will hear from it﴾, i.e., from Jahannam itself, as is the apparent meaning, and this is supported by what follows. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur, the preposition and its object) is connected to a deleted element and functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the words of the Most High ﴿a roaring (shahiqan)﴾, because in origin it was its attribute (sifa). When it became a circumstantial clause, the sense is: ﴿they hear﴾ being ﴿for it a roaring﴾, i.e., a sound like the braying of donkeys, namely its loud, dreadful seething (hasis). In this there is a clear metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya). It is also permitted that the roaring belongs to its people, from those who were previously cast into it, and from themselves, as in the words of the Most High ﴿For them therein is groaning (zafir) and roaring (shahiq)﴾ [Hud: 106]. The speech then involves an elided genitive (hadhf mudaf) or a figurative attribution (tajawwuz fi'l-nisba).

It has been objected that this happens to them only after they settle in the Fire and after it is said to them ﴿Begone therein (ukhsa'u fiha)﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108]. And this occurs after six thousand years from their entry, as in some reports. It was answered that this only indicates that their condition at that time is restricted to groaning and roaring, not that it does not occur from them before that.

﴿تَكادُ تَمَيَّزُ﴾ That is, while the situation is that it boils with them like the boiling of a cauldron with what is in it. ﴿وهِيَ تَفُورُ﴾ That is, parts of it separate from other parts ﴿مِنَ الغَيْظِ﴾ from the intensity of anger against them. Al-Raghib said: "al-Ghayz is the most intense anger." Al-Marzuqi said in al-Fasih: "It is anger, or its worst form." The burning of the fire against them is compared, in the strength of its effect on them and in delivering harm to them, to the rage of an enraged person against another whom he is eager to harm. This is an explicit metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya). It is also permissible that here there is an imaginative metaphor (takhyiliyya) that follows an implicit metaphor (makniyya), by comparing Hell, in the intensity of its boiling and the strength of its effect on its people, to a person who is extremely enraged at another and eager to inflict harm on him. Thus a form is imagined for it like the form of a certain, realized emotional state, namely the anger that drives such conduct, and this imagined state is borrowed for the notion of ghayz.

It is also permitted that the attribution in ﴿تَكادُ تَمَيَّزُ﴾ to Hell is figurative, and the real attribution is to the angels of punishment (al-zabaniyya). It is also possible that the speech contains an elision (taqdir mudaf), meaning: "its guardians (zabaniyyatuha) separate from it out of rage." It has also been said that God Most High creates in it a capacity for perception, so that it becomes enraged at them, and then there is no metaphor in any respect. Some reports support this. Some have claimed that none of what has been mentioned is necessary because of the word ﴿تَكادُ﴾, as in the saying of God Most High ﴿يَكادُ زَيْتُها يُضِيءُ ولَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نارٌ﴾ [al-Nur: 35] (its oil would almost give light even if no fire touched it). But there is much to be said about this.

The sentence is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿تَفُورُ﴾, or another predicate.

Talha read تَتَمَيَّزُ with two tas. Abu 'Amr read تَكادُ تَمَيَّزُ with the dal assimilated into the ta' (idgham). Al-Dahhak read تَمايَزُ on the pattern tafa''ala, whose original form is tatamayyazu with two tas. Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn Abi 'Abla read تَمِيزُ from maza.

﴿كُلَّما أُلْقِيَ فِيها فَوْجٌ﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), brought to explain the condition of its people after explaining its own condition. It has been said that it explains another condition of its people. It is also permitted that the sentence be a circumstantial clause from its pronoun, meaning: "Whenever a group of the disbelievers is cast into it." ﴿سَألَهم خَزَنَتُها﴾ Its guardians, namely Malik and his assistants, peace be upon them, asked them. The questioner may be one or many. The question is not a question of seeking information but a question of rebuke and reproach, and in it there is a spiritual punishment for them, added to their bodily punishment. ﴿ألَمْ يَأْتِكم نَذِيرٌ﴾ Did no warner come to you, who recites to you the signs of God and warns you of the meeting of this your Day?

[page 11]

﴿They will say﴾, acknowledging that He, Mighty and Majestic, has completely removed their excuses, ﴿"Yes, indeed, a warner did come to us."﴾ They combined the particle of response with the very same clause being answered, for emphasis in acknowledging the coming of the warner, and out of regret over the happiness they had missed through their disbelief, and as a preface to the neglect they had committed, feeling remorse and grief over it. That is, each group of those groups said: a warner had come to them, meaning one warner, either in reality or in judgment, like the warning of the Children of Israel, for they are in the position of one warner, so he warned us and recited to us what God Most High had sent down of His verses.

﴿So we denied﴾ that warner, coming from Him, Most High, ﴿and we said﴾, concerning what he recited of the verses, excessively in denial and persistently in rejection, ﴿"God has not sent down anything"﴾ to anyone ﴿of any kind﴾, let alone sending down verses to a human being like you. ﴿"You are only"﴾, that is, you are not, in your claim to what you assert, ﴿"in a great error"﴾, far from truth and correctness.

He used the plural form of the second-person pronoun, although the addressee of each group is its own warner, for the sake of *taghlib* (giving precedence to the dominant or collective form over the others), and even hypothetically, so that it would include the first group to whom a warner was sent. The original sense is: "You and those like you, of those who have claimed or who claim your claim," for emphasis in denial and persistence in misguidance, as indicated by the generality of "what was sent down" together with the omission of mention of the one upon whom it was sent down, for it inherently hints at its generality. As for making the denial of the one stand in place of the denial of all, it was said that it is a real matter to which recourse is made in order to magnify the crime they committed; but there is no room for considering it from their side, nor for including it within their expression.

How could it be otherwise, since it depends on observing the agreement of the warnings upon what does not differ among the laws and rulings despite the differences of eras and years? And where are they from that, when the choking has prevented the recitation? This is if what was mentioned is taken as a report about each one of the groups, as is the apparent meaning. But if it is taken as a report about all of them, then "warner" is either in the sense of a plural, because it is on the pattern *fa'il*, which applies to the singular and to others, or it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) estimated with a general genitive construction (*mudaf*), meaning "the people of a warning," or it is described by it for emphasis, so that both sides of the address agree in plurality. Some expressions suggest that it is permissible to consider the plurality by one of the aspects mentioned, in the first case as well, and this is open to discussion.

It has also been allowed that the address may be from the speech of the guardians of Hell to the disbelievers, with an implied "saying," and that by "error" they mean what they were upon in the world, or their destruction, or the punishment for their error, naming it by the name of its cause; but this is contrary to the apparent meaning, as is not hidden. Likewise is what has been said about the permissibility of it being from the speech of the warner to the disbelievers, whom he reported to the guardians. In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: "This aspect here involves clear artificiality. Either it is the object of an omitted verb implied by 'a warner did come to us,' as if it were said: 'Yes, a warner did come to us, and said: You are only in a great error,' so 'we denied and we said' is put forward to indicate that the denial was not limited to this statement of theirs; or the denial falls on the clause, namely 'You are only,' and His saying, glorified is He, 'and we said: God has not sent down anything,' is coordinated with 'we denied,' placed before its complement so that it functions as a parenthetical interjection, emphasizing the ruling of denial and also indicating non-restriction. The first is preferable." End of quotation.

It has been cited as evidence from this verse that there is no obligation (*taklif*) before the sending of a messenger (*ba'tha*). Interpreting "warner" as the proofs present in the intellects is something no fair-minded person of sound reason would accept.

And they will say, also acknowledging that they were not among those who listened or reasoned: "As if the guardians said to them, amid the rebuke, 'Did you not hear the signs of your Lord and fail to reason about their meanings?' So they answered them with their words: ﴿Had we been listening﴾ to speech ﴿or reasoning﴾
[Page 12]
about anything, ﴿we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze﴾, meaning, among their number and of their company." The intended referents are said to be the devils, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾. It is also said that they are the disbelievers in general. Restricting the preparation of the Blaze to them is disputed, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blaze﴾ [al-Insan: 4]. The verse does not indicate restriction. In this there is a subtle point that you may recognize from what comes soon, God willing, so do not be negligent.

Their negation of hearing and reason is because they treated what they had of them as nonexistent, since they gained no benefit from it. Along with considering the generality of "what is heard" and "what is reasoned," this contains an exaggeration that is evident. Some of the great scholars considered the two as specific, saying: that is, "Had we been listening to the speech of the warner, accepting it entirely without inquiry or investigation, relying on what appeared of its truthfulness through the miracle, or reasoning, so that we would reflect on its wisdom and meanings as discerning people reflect, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze, etc." This contains an indication that hearing and reason here mean acceptance and reflection. The "or" (aw) is for alternation, since the negation of each of them is sufficient for their deliverance from the Blaze; or it is for enumeration, so it does not contradict combination.

It is also said that the verse points to the two types of faith, the imitative (taqlidi) and the verified (tahqiqi), or to the devotional rulings and others. Ibn al-Sam'ani, in his book al-Qawati', said that whoever holds that reason is the arbiter used the verse as evidence. You know that the most it indicates is that reason guides to the correct beliefs by which deliverance from the difficult is achieved, but as for it indicating that reason is the arbiter, as the Mu'tazilah (a theological school) say, it does not. It has also been used as evidence, as reported from Ibn al-Munayyir, that hearing is superior to sight. It is strange that some have used it to argue that one should not call the disbeliever "intelligent" ('aqil).

"So they will acknowledge their sin," which is their disbelief and their denial of the signs of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, and His warners. "So away with the companions of the Blaze" — that is, far away from His mercy, the Exalted; and it is a supplication against them.

Abu Ja'far and al-Kisa'i read "fasuḥqan" (فَسُحْقًا) with a ḍamma on the ḥā' (Ḥ), and suḥq (السُّحْقُ) absolutely means distance. Its being in the accusative is because it is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkad), meaning: Allah distanced them with a distancing. The poet said:

*He roams the far regions of the lands, westward,*
*and the east wind wears him down, every worn-out thing.*

It was also said that it is a verbal noun either of a transitive verb derived from the augmented form by dropping the augmentations, as in His saying:

*If I perish, that was my destiny* (qadarī), meaning my decree (taqdīrī).

And the construction is: "fa-asḥaqahumu Allāhu suḥqan," meaning isḥāqan (causing to be distanced). Or it is a verbal noun of a verb that follows from that verb, meaning: "fa-asḥaqahumu Allāhu ta'ala fa-suḥiqū suḥqan," as in His saying:

*And the bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left nothing of the wealth except what was scraped away or what was stripped bare.*

That is, time has left nothing, so there remained only what was scraped away. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and al-Zajjaj went with the first of the two options. And after establishing the triliteral transitive verb, as in the verse, Abu Hayyan said it does not need what was mentioned.

The lām in "li-aṣḥāb" (لأصحاب) is for specification (lil-tabyin), as in "hayta laka" (هَيْتَ لَكَ) [Yusuf: 23] and "saqyan laka" (سَقْيًا لَكَ). In the verse, according to what has been said, there is taghlib (predominance of one group over another). Its rationale, in the view of the one who said it, is that the context would require saying "fasuḥqan lahum wa li-aṣḥāb al-sa'ir," for Allah first described the condition of the devils when He, glorified be He, said: "And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze" (al-sa'ir). Then He described the condition of the disbelievers when He, Exalted and Majestic, said: "And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell." The more suitable reading with the naṣb (accusative) reading, and the one further from the suspicion of repetition, is that the relative pronoun is meant to refer to other than the devils. Then the Exalted said: "So away with the companions of the Blaze." It is as though the context requires "so away with them and with the companions of the Blaze," but it was not said that way, for the sake of taghlib, since the companions of the Blaze is applied to the devils and the disbelievers together.

There is no harm in this from the indication of other verses that the companions of the Blaze are not restricted to the devils, but it is also applied to the rest of the disbelievers. For what is sufficient for taghlib is the restriction that is evident from the context here. Nor does it depend on the impermissibility of applying that to others than the devils in any of the contexts. Moreover, it is possible to say that there is no need to commit to restricting the companions of the Blaze to the devils at all, even according to the context. Rather, it is sufficient for the soundness of the interpretation that they are the original inhabitants of the Blaze, while the disbelievers are attached to them, as His saying, Exalted be He, indicates: "We were not among the companions of the Blaze," meaning among their numbers and totality. Then the one entering the Blaze becomes two categories.

The apparent requirement was to mention both of them together in the supplication against them with distance, as the context of the verse witnesses. But He adjusted it and gave predominance to "companions of the Blaze," which indicates originality, over the others of the followers. He mentioned that in this predominance there is brevity, which is evident, and hyperbole, that is, in the distancing. For if each of the two groups had been mentioned separately, it could have been supposed that the distancing differs, such that the distancing of the disbelievers is less than the distancing of the devils, in accordance with what is indicated by making the devils the originals and themselves attached to them. So when they were joined to them in the ruling of it, it showed that their distancing did not fall short of that of those. Also, when Allah, glorified and exalted be He, gave predominance to the companions of the Blaze, who are the devils, over the disbelievers, He made the disbelievers of the kind of the devils, so that they are as they themselves are. In this there is hyperbole that is not hidden. And [there is] causation (ta'lil), for the anticipation of the ruling upon the attribute, and likewise its connection to it, indicates that the attribute is its cause. So that indicates that the distancing occurred to them because of their being companions of the Blaze.

Others have said regarding the justification of the taghlib and the three matters within it other than this, and that has been counted among the difficulties and has become a battleground for the scholars of Rum and other eminent scholars. Perhaps what we have mentioned is closer to understanding and further from dispute and contention. So reflect, and Allah, the Exalted, is the Protector of understanding.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen⦅bil-ghayb⦆, for them is forgiveness﴾ means: they fear His punishment while it is absent from them, or while they are absent from it, or [they fear Him] away from the eyes of people, not showing off, or [the meaning is] "with that which is hidden from them," which is their hearts. ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, great, for their sins, ﴿and a great reward﴾ whose magnitude cannot be measured. The placing of forgiveness before the reward is because warding off harms is more important than acquiring benefits. And the sentence mentioned has been said to be a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 13:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And keep your speech secret or divulge it﴾, is an address of general application to all the morally responsible (mukallafun), as in His earlier saying ﴿that He may test you﴾. It is conjoined (ʿatf) to an implied clause. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: the original sense of the discourse is: "And for those of you who disbelieve, O you who are responsible and under trial, and for those of you who fear..." Then the second part was cut off as an answer to a question that arises from the description of the state of the disbelievers, although their mention is incidental (bi-l-ʿaraḍ), namely: what is the state of those who act best, and who emerge purified (mumahhasan) at the time of trial? So he was answered with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who fear﴾ etc. Thus He established for them perfect knowledge, ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28], and perfect piety, by His saying ﴿in the unseen﴾. In this cutting off there is a further clarification (tarshih) of the meaning alluded to in His saying ﴿which of you is best in deed﴾, that is: ﴿that He may test you, which of you﴾ is the pious one, singling them out as the intended ones. Had it been conjoined, it would have indicated equality. Then it was said: "So fear Him in secret and in public, and persist, you who are humble, in your fear, and turn in repentance to fear and piety, you who are deluded, and believe that your secrets and your openness are equal in the knowledge of your Lord. So be on guard and fear Him with the fear due to Him." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿That﴾ is thus conjoined to this implied clause.

It is also permissible to make His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who﴾ etc. a digression (istitrad) following the mention of the disbelievers and their recompense, and His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿And keep your speech secret﴾ and ﴿or divulge it﴾, by way of iltifat (shift of address) to the companions of the blaze, because of the distance of the reference and the increase of specificity, conjoined to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And for those who disbelieve﴾, as if it were said: "And for the disbelievers in their Lord is the punishment of Hell." Then it was said, describing it: such and such. "Your keeping speech secret and your divulging it, O disbelievers, are alike, so you will not escape Us, whether you openly profess disbelief and hatred, or conceal them both, which is part of the threat." Then he said: "The first is more acceptable." The first, however, appears to me to be far-fetched, and the second is supported by what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The verses ﴿And keep your speech secret﴾ etc. were revealed concerning the polytheists who used to revile the Prophet ﷺ, and revelation would come to him, peace be upon him. Some of them said to others: 'Keep your speech secret, lest the Lord of Muhammad hear.' So it was said to them: 'Keep it secret or divulge it, for indeed Allah knows it.'"

The placing of secrecy before divulgence serves to announce their exposure and the befalling of what they fear from the very beginning, and to emphasize the comprehensiveness of the knowledge of the Mighty, the Majestic, which encompasses all that is known. It is as if His knowledge, exalted is He, of what they keep secret is prior to what they divulge, although in reality the two are on a par. Alternatively, the rank of secrecy precedes the rank of divulgence, for there is nothing divulged except that it, or its beginnings, is generally concealed in the heart. Thus His knowledge, exalted is He, of its first state precedes His knowledge of its second state.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, He is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾ is a causal explanation (taʿlil) of what precedes it and a confirmation of it. In the form faʿil (ʿalim), and in the adornment of "the breasts" with the definite article of comprehensiveness (lam al-istighraq), and in the description of the inner thoughts by their possessor, there is an eloquence that is not hidden: it is as if it were said: "Indeed, He, the Mighty, the Majestic, is exceedingly thorough in encompassing the concealed thoughts of all people and their hidden secrets lodged in their breasts, to the point that they scarcely ever depart from them at all. How, then, would He not know what you keep secret and what you divulge?" It is also permissible that by "what is within the breasts" is meant the hearts that are in the breasts, and the meaning is that He, exalted is He, is ﴿Knower﴾ of hearts and their states, so no secret of theirs is hidden from Him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Should not He who created know?﴾ is a denial and negation of the non-comprehensiveness of His knowledge, exalted be His majesty. The agent of "knows" is understood as: should not He who brought into being, in accordance with the requirement of His wisdom, all things, of which these (the secret and the open) are part, know the secret and the open?

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the agent of "knows," emphasizing the denial and negation. That is: should He not know that, while He, may He be exalted, is the one whose knowledge reaches what appears of His creation and what is hidden within it? It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause relating to the agent of "created," but the first is more apparent. The object of "knows" is estimated as stated above. The verb was not treated as belonging to the category of "gives and withholds" (i.e., a verb whose object may be omitted), because of the position of this circumstantial clause, as has been said. For if you said, "Should not he who is a creator not be knowing, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware," it would not be a correct meaning, since "should not know" depends on the circumstantial clause, and a thing is not restricted by itself. So one does not say, "Should he not know while he is knowing," but rather, "Should he not know such-and-such while he is knowing every thing." It was objected to this that al-Latif is the one who knows the hidden things, so the meaning would be: should he not be knowing while he knows the hidden things? And this is sound. It was answered that "does not know" is of that category, and it is, according to what al-Sakkaki established, absorbed in the rhetorical context (al-maqam al-khitabi). ("The Subtle, the All-Aware") is one whose knowledge reaches what appears of His creation and what is hidden within it. Thus the two are equal in comprehensiveness and generality.

It was rebutted that comprehensiveness is not necessary, as al-Zamakhshari mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], the verse. And even if it is granted, the aspect differs, because the generality derived from the second is not the generality derived from the first, for the subtlety pertains specifically to the knowledge of hidden things, while knowledge of manifest things follows by way of implication. Furthermore, al-Ghazali considered in the concept of al-Latif, together with knowledge of the hidden matters, the course of gentleness in conveying what sets them right; thus it is not repeated with al-Khabir, on the basis that the latter is also the knower of hidden things.

As for the need for the estimate, as some of the imams have said: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Should not He know?﴾ is a concluding generalization (tadhyil) after the causal explanation given in His saying, glorified be He, ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾. The connection of meaning is that it may be said: "Should not He know this hidden matter, I mean your speech which you keep private, or should not He know your secret and your open speech, He who knows the subtleties of hidden things and their grand matters, their totalities and their details?" Had it been said, "Should not he who is such be a knower of perfect knowledge?", it would not be connected, and there would be in it weakness and deficiency. He (al-Alusi) allowed that "man" (man) be the object of "created" and Abu Hayyan favored this, meaning: should He not know His creation, while this is His state? He preferred the first, on the ground that in it there is the placing of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun referring to the Lord, and it is more indicative of the omitted object, I mean the secret and the open, and the generalization of "created," which encompasses both of them in an initial manner. For this reason they estimated "who created things," as an indication that the omission of the object is for generality.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 15:

﴿He is the One Who made the earth docile (dhalul) for you﴾, not difficult, so that traversing it is very easy for you. Thus dhalul is an intensive form (fa'ul, for mubalagha) from dhull (with a damma, and it may be read with a kasra), the opposite of hardness (su'ubah). The form with a damma is used for what is opposed to honour (izz), as the wording of the Qamus requires. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: dhalul is fa'ul in the sense of maf'ul, i.e. madhulah, like rakub and halub, end quote. It was objected that its verb is intransitive, and it is only made transitive by the hamza or by doubling, so it cannot mean maf'ul; and he (al-Alusi) judged that madhulah is an error. Some of them said: they say of a riding animal when it is compliant and not difficult, dhalul, from dhill (with a kasra), which is ease of submission. In the phrase there is a metaphor (isti'arah), and it has been said to be an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh). The word "for you" (lakum) is placed before the two objects of the verb "made" although its proper place is after them, for the sake of emphasis on what is fronted and to create anticipation for what is delayed; for what should be fronted, when delayed, especially when the fronted element indicates that the delayed element is one of the benefits for the addressees, keeps the soul anticipating its arrival, so that it settles deeply upon mention of it.

The fa' in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So walk in its shoulders﴾, is for ordering the command upon the mentioned making. Some claimed that it is fa'sihah (an expressive fa'). The intended meaning of "its shoulders" (manakibiha), as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others, is: its mountains. Al-Hasan said: its roads and its passes. The original meaning of mankib is the joint between the upper arm and the shoulder blade, and its use in this sense is by way of explicit (tasrihiyyah) and substantive (tahqiqiyyah) metaphor, and it is the companion (qarinah) of the implicit metaphor (makniyyah) in "the earth", where it has been likened to a camel, as al-Khafaji mentioned. Then he said: If you say, how can it be implicit when its other side has been mentioned in His words, ﴿docile﴾? I say: it is by the estimate "an earth that is docile", so what is mentioned is the generic earth in absolute terms, while the likened thing is the particular external individual, which is not mentioned; therefore "docile" may be a metaphor, and the implicit metaphor is then the referent of the pronoun, not what is explicitly stated in the noble text. What prevents metaphor is the mention of the likened thing itself, not of what applies to it; so reflect and do not be heedless.

In al-Kashshaf: walking "in its shoulders" is a proverb for extreme subjugation and going beyond the limit, because the two shoulders and their junction on the back of a camel are the most delicate part of it, and it is far removed from being trodden on by a rider's foot and relied upon. It leaves no remnant of subjugation. The intended meaning is that there is no actual command to walk here; rather the aim is to make it a proverb for extreme subjugation, whether the shoulders are interpreted as mountains or otherwise, and whether what precedes is a metaphor or a simile. ﴿And eat of His provision﴾: benefit from what He, mighty is His majesty, has bestowed. Often the various forms of benefit are expressed by eating, because it is the most important and most general.

In Anwar al-Tanzil: i.e., seek from the blessings of God, glorified and exalted is He, with eating being a metaphor for seeking, of the kind of mentioning the necessary concomitant while intending the consequent. It was said: this is the suitable reading in view of His words "walk". Some allowed keeping it on its literal sense, on the basis that this belongs to the category of sufficiency (al-iktifa'), but it is not that.

The verse is cited as evidence for the recommendation (nadb) of seeking means and earning.

In a hadith: "Indeed God, exalted is He, loves the believing servant who works at a trade (al-muhtarif)."

This does not contradict reliance on God (tawakkul). Rather, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related from Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, passed by a people and said: "Who are you?" They said: "The reliant ones (al-mutawakkilun)." He said: "You are rather the ones who depend on others (al-mutakkilun). The one who relies upon God is a man who casts his seed into the belly of the earth and relies upon his Lord, mighty and majestic."

The full discussion of this section belongs in its proper place. The well-known view is that the command in both places is for permission (ibahah), but it has been allowed that it is for absolute request, since walking and what is conjoined to it include what is obligatory, as is not hidden.

﴿And to Him is the resurrection﴾, i.e., the return after the resurrection, not to any other, mighty and majestic is He. So exert yourselves in thanking His blessings, among which is the subjugation of the earth, your being enabled upon it, and the dispersal of provision in it. Among what is strange in this is the permissibility of the pronoun in "His provision" referring to the earth, by considering it as a source or an element of the elements, or as docile, and the word is the same for masculine and feminine; and the attribution is for the slightest connection, i.e., of the provision which He created upon it.
