Likewise the pronoun in "to Him" means: and to the earth is your rising and your return, so you will come out from your houses and palaces to your graves. The clause "and to Him is the resurrection" has been said to be a conjunction upon the relative clause after considering what follows from it, and it has been said to be a circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from the pronoun of the addressees in the nominative; so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 16:

﴿Are you secure that He who is in the heaven...﴾ is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as one of many scholars held. It was said, interpreting ﴿He who is in the heaven﴾ as: His command and His decree, meaning that it is a metonymy in the attribution, or that there is an implied omitted genitive (muḍāf), and its original form is "He who is in the heaven [His] command." When the muḍāf was omitted and the muḍāf ilayhi took its place, it took the nominative case and became concealed. It was also said: "on the assumption of the Creator of He who is in the heaven." It was also said: "fī" (in) here means "ʿalā" (upon), and what is meant is elevation through domination and power. It was also said that it is based on the belief of the Arabs, for they used to assume that He, glorified be He, is in the heaven; so it is as if it were said: "Are you secure from the One whom you assume to be ﴿in the heaven﴾, while He is exalted above place?" This is in the utmost feebleness, for how would it be fitting to construct speech in such a context upon the assumption of some of the ignorant, as is not hidden from the fair-minded? Or the referent is other than Him, Mighty is His station, and some have gone to this, saying: what is meant by the relative clause is the angels, peace be upon them, who are entrusted with managing this world. It was also said: Jibril, peace be upon him, who is the angel entrusted with the sinking of the earth. The leading scholars of the early generations did not go to anything other than Allah, exalted is He, and the verse, according to them, is among the mutashabihat (ambiguous verses). The Prophet ﷺ said: "Believe in its ambiguous parts."

They did not say: interpret it. Rather, they believe that He, Mighty and Majestic, is in the heaven in the sense that He, glorified be He, intended, along with complete transcendence. The hadith of the slave-girl is among the strongest proofs for them in this matter, and interpreting it by what Ibn al-Khalaf interpreted is a departure from the circle of fairness in the view of people of understanding. In Fath al-Bari by the Hafiz Ibn Hajar, al-Lalika'i is cited, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani, who said: All the jurists, from the East to the West, agree on belief in the Qur'an and the hadiths which the trustworthy transmitters have related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning the attributes of the Lord, without likening Him to anything and without interpretation (tafsir).

Al-Bayhaqi cited with a sound chain, from Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari, from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna: Whatever Allah, exalted is He, described Himself with in His Book, its explanation is its recitation and remaining silent about it. This is the method of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

Imam al-Haramayn said in al-Risala al-Nizamiyya: The methods of the scholars differed regarding these apparent meanings. Some of them held to interpreting them and adopted that for the verses of the Book and the authentic Sunnas. The leading scholars of the early generations went to refraining from interpretation, letting the apparent meanings stand on their own footing and committing their meanings to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. What we approve as an opinion, and adopt as a creed before Allah, exalted is He, is following the predecessors of the community, on the decisive proof that the consensus of the community is binding. Had the interpretation of these apparent meanings been obligatory, their concern with it would have been likely to exceed their concern with the branches of the Sharia; since the era of the Companions and the Successors passed with turning away from interpretation, that was the followed path. End of the Imam's words.

The transmission on this has already been mentioned from the people of the third era, who are the jurists of the cities, such as al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Malik, al-Layth, and those contemporary with them, and likewise those from the Imams who took from them. How, then, would what the people of the three generations agreed upon not be trusted, and they are the best generations by the testimony of the Lawgiver, upon whom be prayers and peace? End of the Hafiz's words, in summary.

He cited the texts of the Imams on applying this to its apparent meaning along with transcendence, without interpretation, which would lead to considerable elaboration and length. Notable books have been composed on this, both extensive and concise. In Tanbih al-'Uqul by our shaykh of shaykhs Ibrahim al-Kurani, it is stated that the consensus of the three generations on applying the ambiguous expressions to their (apparent) referents, along with transcendence by ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11], is evidence that the Lawgiver, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, intended their apparent meanings; and the certainty of his truthfulness ﷺ is evidence of the absence of any rational counter-argument indicating the opposite of what the transmitted proof indicates in reality, even if the rational person imagines it in the stage of reflection and thought. Thus knowing Allah by this kind of attributes is a stage beyond that. End of quotation.

I say: interpretation is following conjecture and speaking about Allah, Mighty and Majestic, without knowledge; otherwise, what they mention as the meaning would be unified, whereas the matter is not so, since they mention for one thing several possible meanings. In what the predecessors adhered to there is safety from that, and this suffices to show it is the best of paths.

And what is upon me, if I say my belief, leave the ignorant one who thinks ignorance is enmity.

Nafi' read "a-amintum" with the first hamza realized and the second softened, and Abu 'Amr and Qalun inserted an alif between them. Qunbul read by changing the first to a waw because of the damma before it, which is the ra' of al-nushur; and other readings from him and from Warsh also exist.

His Exalted saying ﴿an yakhsifa bikumu al-ardh﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from ﴿man﴾. It was also permitted that it be by omitting the preposition, i.e., "min an yakhsifa," and its position is then in the accusative or genitive; the bāʾ is for accompaniment, and "al-ardh" is the object of "yakhsifa." Khasf may be transitive. Al-Raghib said: it is said "khasafahu Allah" and "khasafa huwa," and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾ [al-Qasas: 81]. That is: Are you secure from His causing the earth to go down to a lower place while you are in it? Some claimed the necessity of its necessity and that "al-ardh" is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., "an yakhsifa bikum fi al-ardh"; but that is not so. ﴿Then behold, it﴾, at the time of the sinking, ﴿shakes﴾, it quakes and trembles violently; and the root of mawr is repeated movement in coming and going.

Al-Alusi's commentary on surah 67, verse 17:

﴿Or are you secure from He who is in the heaven, that He will not send against you a violent wind (ḥāṣib)?﴾ This is an *idrāb* (a shift of discourse, a turn from one threat to another) from the earlier threat to a threat of a different kind. The meaning is: "Rather, are you secure from He who is in the heaven, that He will send…" and so on. The discussion of the ḥāṣib and of the threat of *khasf* (the earth swallowing them) was given earlier, because of the mention of the earth in His saying, ﴿He it is who made the earth subservient to you, so walk in its broad tracts and eat of His provision﴾. In that verse He mentioned the favour of making walking easy in its tracts. Here, the sending of the ḥāṣib is mentioned second, in response to the favour expressed in His saying, ﴿and eat of His provision﴾. Do you not see His saying, ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 22]? This is stated in al-Kashshāf.

In Ghurrat al-Tanzīl, al-Rāghib gives the reason for placing the threat of *khasf* before the threat of the ḥāṣib: since the earth, which God spread out for them to settle on and worship their Creator in, was the place in which they worshipped idols, which were of its trees or its stones, they were warned with what was closer to them. The warning of the ḥāṣib from the heaven, which is the channel for their good words and the ascent-route of their righteous deeds, was because they had exchanged these for the evil of their disbelief and their foul deeds. Yet what was indicated earlier is perhaps the better explanation.

﴿Then you will know how My warning was﴾, that is, how My *inḏār* (warning) was. Here *nadhīr* is a verbal noun of the same pattern, as in the verse of Ḥassān:

"So I warn her (Quraysh) sincerely on behalf of the Most Merciful, if she accepts my warning."

It is *muḍāf* (in construct) to the pronoun-suffix *yā'* (my), and the readers differ regarding it. Some of them omit it in pausal and connected speech alike, retaining it in neither, while others omit it in connected speech and keep it in pause. Others omit it in both states, relying on the *kasra* (the vowel) as an indicator. The meaning is: "Then you will know what my warning was like, and my power to carry it out, when you witness that with which you are warned. But knowledge will not benefit you at that time." It has also been read irregularly (*shādhdh*) as *fa-sayaʿlamūna*, with the *yā'* of the third person.

[Page 17]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 18:

﴿And indeed, those before them denied,﴾ i.e., before the disbelievers of Makkah, from among the disbelievers of the earlier nations: the people of Nuh (Noah), 'Ad, and their likes. The shift to the third person (al-iltifat ila al-ghaybah) is to express disregard for them (li-ibrar al-i'rad 'anhum).

﴿So how was My denial (nakir)?﴾ i.e., My disapproval of them through the sending down of punishment, meaning it was of the utmost terror and severity. This is the place of the emphasis by oath, not merely their denial. The discussion of ﴿نَكِيرِ﴾ (nakir) is like the discussion of ﴿نَذِيرِ﴾ (nadhir), and in the speech there is an abundance of emphasis in consoling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and intensifying the threat to his people, which is not hidden.

﴿Have they not seen﴾: they were heedless and did not look ﴿at the birds above them, spreading their wings﴾ extended in the air as they fly. When they spread them, they align their primary feathers (qawadim), meaning the feathers that project forward, in a row. ﴿Spreading﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating either to the birds or to the pronoun in ﴿above them﴾, which itself occupies the position of a circumstantial clause, so the circumstantial clauses are interlocked. It is also permissible that it be an adverbial complement of ﴿spreading﴾ or of ﴿have they not seen﴾. The object of ﴿spreading﴾ is omitted under these possibilities, as we have indicated.

The mention of taking warning from the birds suits the mention of the threat of the hasiba (a shower of stones), especially if it is interpreted as stones, since God Almighty destroyed the People of the Elephant with that when the birds pelted them. In that there is a reminder to the Quraysh of that story. ﴿And folding﴾: and gathering in their wings when they strike their sides with them. The conjunction with ﴿spreading﴾ is because the meaning is "they spread and fold," or "spreading and folding." Conjoining a verb to a noun in such a construction is eloquent and common, and the reverse is permissible and good, except according to al-Suhayli, who considers it ugly. An example is his saying:

"He spent the night covering her with a keen, cutting sword, aiming at her shanks and her... wandering."

He intended "qasid wa jair" (a noun followed by a noun). Since the essence of flight is the alignment of the wings, because flying in the air is like swimming in water, and its basis is the extension and spreading of the limbs, while folding is a secondary act added to spreading to aid movement, the verb was used for what is an accidental act, and the noun for what is the essence. The meaning is that they are spreading, and from them folding occurs at times, one after another, renewing itself from time to time, just as a swimmer does. ﴿What holds them﴾ up in the air during spreading and folding, contrary to the natural tendency of heavy bodies to descend to the earth and be drawn towards it: ﴿except the Most Merciful﴾, whose mercy encompasses everything, since He created them in forms and characteristics and inspired in them movements by which running in the air became possible.

The clause is either a new independent sentence or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (yaqbid'na). al-Zuhri read ﴿what holds them﴾ with shadda (emphatic doubling). ﴿Indeed He is, of everything, All-Seeing﴾: of subtle knowledge, so He, glorified and exalted, knows how creatures are originated and how created things are arranged. Whoever has such creation as God, Mighty and Majestic, has given the bird, so that its running in the air is possible, while He is capable of making it run in it without that, yet wisdom required linking effects to their causes. Nothing in what we have mentioned inclines towards what is harmful from the sayings of the natural philosophers, because the fact that heavy bodies have the nature you heard about is a sensible matter that none denies except one who disputes his own senses. Similar is that holding is by the prior cause, and that it is a cause among the effects of His vast mercy, exalted be He.

Abu Hayyan rejected this, supposing it to be an inclination towards what is harmful from the sayings of the natural philosophers, and said: "We say that if God, glorified be He, wills to hold the heaviest things in the air and raise them up to the Throne, that happens; and if He, exalted be His majesty, wills to lower what is lighter in its lowest part to the furthest point it descends, that also happens. That is not due to shape, weight, or lightness. We do not deny that God, exalted be He, is capable of all things, that He, glorified be He, does whatever He wills, and that His action, Mighty and Majestic, is not rationally dependent on a cause. Yet we say that His wisdom, exalted be He, required that linking in this world, and it is a customary matter that He chose, exalted be He, out of wisdom and grace. Had He, glorified and exalted, willed other than it, it would have been as He willed."

The placing of ﴿of everything﴾ before ﴿All-Seeing﴾ is for the rhyme (fasila), or for restriction, in refutation of one who claims that His knowledge, exalted be His majesty, does not encompass everything.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 20:**

﴿Or who is it that is an army for you to help you, apart from the Most Merciful?﴾ According to many scholars, this is connected to the Exalted's words ﴿Have they not considered the birds?﴾. Al-Bayda'i (*al-Irshad*, the work of Abu al-Su'ud, is what is meant here) said: "It is a rebuke to them, by denying that they have any helper other than God, the Exalted, as is suggested by the choice of the title 'the Most Merciful' and reinforced by His words ﴿None holds them up except the Most Merciful﴾." Or it means: "a helper against His punishment, the Exalted," which is the most fitting reading in light of His words after He has withheld His provision, like His words ﴿Or do they have gods that protect them from Us?﴾ (al-Anbiya': 43). Both meanings are intended together, except that the interrogation there is directed at the protector himself, while its realization here is directed at identifying the helper, in order to rebuke them by showing their inability to name him.

*Am* (أمْ) here is an implied *munqati'ah* (disjunctive) particle, equivalent in meaning to *bal* (بَلْ, "rather"), marking a transition from rebuking them for failing to reflect on what they see of the birds, which point to the wondrous signs of God's power, to the rebuke expressed in what was mentioned. The *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person) serves to intensify this rebuke. There is no way to posit a hamzah (interrogative particle) with it, because it is followed by *man* (مَنِ), the interrogative pronoun, and an interrogative does not enter upon another interrogative in the known usage. *Man* is a *mubtada'* (subject), and *hadha* (هَذا) is its *khabar* (predicate). Regarding the relative pronoun here, the well-known possibilities for such a construction apply.

The clause ﴿yansurukum﴾ (helps you) is an attribute (*sifah*) of *jund* (army) in terms of its wording. ﴿min dun al-Rahman﴾ (apart from the Most Merciful), according to the first reading, is either a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from the subject of ﴿yansurukum﴾ or a qualifier (*na't*) of its verbal noun. According to the second reading, it is connected to ﴿yansurukum﴾, as in the Exalted's words ﴿Who will help me against God?﴾ (Hud: 63). The meaning is: "Who is this insignificant one who, in your claim, is an army for you, helping you beyond the help of the Most Merciful? Or who helps you with a help that exists apart from His help, the Exalted? Or who helps you from a punishment that comes from God, the Exalted and Majestic?"

His words, the Exalted, ﴿The disbelievers are only in delusion﴾ are a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) that confirms what precedes it and condemns them for their extreme error. That is, they claim that they are protected from calamities by the protection of their gods, not by His protection alone, and that their gods guard them from the might of God, the Exalted, only in a great delusion and a shameful misguidance originating from Satan, in which they have nothing worth considering in any respect. The shift to the third person (*ghaybah*) signals that their condition calls for turning away from them and for making their ugly qualities known to others. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to censure them for disbelief and to state the cause of their delusion.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 21:

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or who is this that provides for you if He withholds His provision?﴾ — that is, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, [withholds] His provision by withholding the rain and its various precursors, as has passed. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Rather they persist﴾ and so on, indicates an implied element that the context calls for, as if it were said: the effect of the rebuke and the challenge did not touch them; they did not submit to the truth, but persisted and went on obstinately, ﴿in insolence﴾, that is, in obstinacy, arrogance and transgression, ﴿and aversion﴾, that is, fleeing from the truth because it is heavy upon them. Some have made the phrase ﴿Or who is this that is a host for you, to aid you apart from the Most Merciful?﴾ equivalent to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Have they not seen?﴾, in the sense of: have they not considered such works as grasping, spreading out, and withholding, and what resembles them, which indicate complete power, so that they did not know Our power to punish them by such means as sinking into the earth and the sending of a storm of stones? ﴿Or who is this that is a host for you, to aid you apart from Allah if He sends His punishment upon you?﴾

It has been said that it is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Or have they gods that protect them from Us?﴾, except that it is presented in the form of a question about specifying who will help them, indicating that they believed in this category. And he (al-Zamakhshari) made His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Or who is this that provides for you﴾ and so on, in the sense of: or who is it that is pointed to and it is said, "This is the one who provides for you." It has been said that he, may Allah have mercy on him, made in the first [instance] "am" connective and "man" interrogative, and in the second made "am" disconnective and "man" relative, and "hadha alladhi" (this who) is a subject and predicate functioning as a relative clause, under an implied verb of saying. He considered it objectionable to say "alladhi hadha alladhi yarzuqukum" (who this who provides for you), and makes "hadha" stand in place of the pronoun referring back to the first relative. As for "man" being a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "a provider for you," it seems that he indicated thereby the validity of both possibilities in the two places.

As for the matter of the necessity of the two interrogatives coming together in some forms, and the interrogative entering upon an interrogative, it has been said against this that it is not harmful, since there is no obstacle to two interrogatives coming together when emphasis is intended. Ibn al-Shajari reported from all the Basran grammarians that disconnective "am" is always in the sense of "bal" (rather) plus the hamza (interrogative particle), meaning that even if it enters upon an interrogative, as in ﴿Or is the blind man equal to the seeing?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16] and ﴿Or what were you doing?﴾ [al-Naml: 84].

The position of others is that it may come in the sense of bare interrogation, and this is reported from Abu 'Ubayda, and that it may come for bare reversal (idrab), and may include it along with the denying or demanding interrogative.

Al-Zamakhshari said in both places: "am man yushar ilayhi wa yuqal hadha alladhi," and he allowed in this that it be a pointing to an assumed [group], and that it be a pointing to all the idols, because of their belief that they are protected from calamities and provided for by the blessing of their gods. So they are the host, the helper, and the provider. The verse, according to this, is not connected to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Have they not seen?﴾, as verified by the author of al-Kashf, who said after clarifying his words: When this is established, know that what the arrangement requires according to this explanation is that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Or who is this that is a host﴾ be connected to the account of the sinking, and His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿Or who is this that provides for you﴾ be connected to the account of sending the storm of stones, by way of distribution. As if, when it was said, ﴿Do you feel secure from He who is in the heaven that He will sink the earth with you, and it shakes?﴾ — after being in utmost humiliation — He followed it with "am amankum al-fawj alladhi huwa fi za'mikum huwa jundun lakum yamna'ukum min 'adhab Allah ta'ala wa ba'sihi" (or who is it that has secured you, the group which in your claim is a host for you protecting you from the punishment of Allah, Exalted is He, and His might), with "am" being disconnective and the interrogative being mockery. Likewise, when it was said, ﴿Or do you feel secure from He who is in the heaven that He will send upon you a storm of stones?﴾, instead of "He sends upon you His mercy," he followed it with "am amankum alladhi tatawahhamuna annahu yarzuqukum" (or who is it that has secured you, the one you imagine provides for you).

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And those before them denied﴾, it is an interjection that strengthens the force of the warning, and that among the past nations, those swallowed up and those upon whom the stones were sent, and other kinds of His punishment, Mighty and Majestic, is what would strip them of tranquility and dignity if they took heed. Likewise His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿Have they not seen?﴾ is a depiction of His overwhelming power, and that whoever is capable of that, sinking and the sending of a storm of stones upon him are the easiest of things. In it, as He by His great power and the breadth of His mercy holds the birds aloft, so His withholding the punishment is similar; otherwise these people deserve every chastisement. In bringing this there is a contempt that indicates the foolishness of their opinion, and the implication of saying (a claim) that indicates their assertion, and the emphasis by the two relatives that indicates the firmness of their belief in that falsehood, if it refers to the idols; or the utmost mockery at them, as if they were certain and known, if it refers to an assumed group, because their state of security requires that. This is more eloquent, and for this reason al-Zamakhshari placed it first, as it presents what calls for wonder and manifests the inimitability of the Revelation, as if it were a matter seen with the eye. Then he said: "This is what I was guided to, with the acknowledgment that the acknowledgment is from the currents of the speech of Allah, Exalted is He. There are men far above the likes of me, but I console myself with the words of our imam al-Shafi'i:

I love the righteous, though I am not of them."

He finished. By my life, he has excelled, and what he said has attained the highest station of acceptance among people of intellect. And I am impressed by a man whose tears flow over his lofty virtue; to Allah belongs his excellence.

The apparent meaning is that "man" in both places is the subject of an omitted verb indicated by the context, namely "amman-kum," not a subject whose predicate is omitted, as was said earlier. He also permitted in the verse other possibilities of grammatical analysis beyond those mentioned, namely that "man" be a fronted predicate and "hadha" a subject, and he preferred over what has passed the reverse, because it is free from informing about a definite thing by an indefinite, which is not permissible according to the majority; its permissibility is the view of Sibawayh when the subject is an interrogative noun or an elative (af'al tafdil). Talha read in the first "amman" with a light mim, and stressed the second like the majority.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 67, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Is one who walks prone on his face better guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?﴾ is a parable struck for the polytheist and the monotheist, to clarify their two states in this world and to establish the reality of their two ways. The fa' (the "then" particle) is for ordering this upon what has become apparent of the evil condition of the disbelievers, their falling into the pits of delusion, and their mounting the back of the blind and wild recalcitrance. The hamzah (the interrogative particle) is placed before it in form, but that is only because it demands initial position. In meaning, however, the sense is the reverse, as is well known. Indeed, had the hamzah been replaced by hal (a different interrogative), it would have been said, "So is it that one who walks...", etc.

Man (مَن, "one who") is a relative pronoun functioning as the subject (mubtada'), yamshi (يَمْشِي, "walks") is its relative clause (silah), and mukibban (مُكِبًّا, "prone") is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun concealed within the verb.

ʿalā wajhihi (عَلى وَجْهِهِ, "on his face") is a adverbial phrase (ẓarf laghw) connected to mukibban, or it may be a settled circumstantial phrase (mustaqirr ḥāl). The first is preferable. Ahda (أهْدى, "better guided") is the predicate of man. Man (مَنِ, "one who") in the second position is a conjunction linked to the first, and it is coordination of a single noun with a single noun, as in your saying: "Is Zayd better or ʿAmr?" It has also been said that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, because the predicate of the first clause indicates it, but there is no need for that given what you have heard.

The mukibb (مُكِبّ) is one who has fallen upon his face. It is said: akabba (أكَبَّ, "he fell") on his face, and it is of the category of the verbs with the hamzah (af'āl). The well-known view is that it is intransitive, while its triliteral form is transitive, so it is said: kabbahu (كَبَّهُ, "He made him fall") Allah, may He be exalted, and so he fell (akabba). This has come against the analogical pattern, and it has few parallels, such as amarrat al-naqatu (أمَرَّتِ النّاقَةُ, "the she-camel's milk flowed"), which means durrat (دَرَّتْ, "it gave milk"); marra tihan (مَرَّ تِيهًا, "he strutted with arrogance"); ashnaqa al-baʿir (أشْنَقَ البَعِيرُ, "the camel raised its head") meaning rafaʿa ra'sahu (رَفَعَ رَأسَهُ), and shanaqtuhu (شَنَقْتُهُ, "I made it raise its head"); aqshaʿa al-ghaym (أقْشَعَ الغَيْمُ, "the cloud dispersed") and qashaʿat-hu al-rīḥ (قَشَعَتْهُ الرِّيحُ, "the wind dispersed it"), meaning azālathu (أزالَتْهُ, "removed it") and kashafathu (كَشَفَتْهُ, "uncovered it"); anzafat al-biʾr (أنْزَفَتِ البِئْرُ, "the well was drained") and nazaftuhā (نَزَفْتُها, "I drained it"), meaning it brought out its water; and ansala rīsh al-ṭāʾir (أنْسَلَ رِيشُ الطّائِرِ, "the bird's feathers fell out") and nasaltuhu (نَسَلْتُهُ, "I plucked its feathers").

Some have said: the verified view is that the hamzah in it indicates becoming (ṣayrūrah), so the meaning of akabba is "became one who has a kabb" (a state of being prone), and he entered into it, as in alʾama (ألْأمَ, "he became base") when he became lowly, and infaḍḍa (انْفَضَّ, "he became one who has spent") when he became one who has spent what was in his provision. It is not for the sense of intransitive reflexive (muṭāwaʿah). The reflexive counterpart of kabba is only inkabba (انْكَبَّ). Ibn Sidah held this view in al-Muḥkam, following al-Jawhari and others, and Ibn al-Ḥājib and most commentators of al-Mufaṣṣal followed him. However, the words of some eminent scholars clearly equate the reflexive sense with the sense of becoming. Ibn al-Aʿrabi related: kabbahu Allah (كَبَّهُ اللَّهُ) and akabbahu, both transitively. In al-Qamus there is a text explicitly stating this, and according to it there is no violation of analogy.

The meaning is: "Is one who walks while he stumbles at every moment, and falls upon his face at every step, because of the roughness of his path and the unevenness of its parts, with some parts lowered and others raised, better guided and more rightly directed to the goal he seeks? Or is one who walks upright, safe from stumbling and tripping, on a path whose parts are level, with no crookedness or deviation?" The way of the disbeliever is not stated explicitly. Instead, it is indicated by what shows its roughness and lack of straightness, namely mukibban, to convey that what he is upon should not be called a path.

Some have explained sawiyyan (سَوِيًّا, "upright") as "level in direction, slightly deviating," and that mukibb is one who wanders in this direction and that direction. This is not appropriate here, because His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿on a straight path﴾ would become like a repetition. The elative (af'al, أفعل) here is used as an example, according to what is in al-Bahr, in your saying: "Honey is sweeter than vinegar."

The verse, according to what is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), was revealed concerning Abu Jahl (may the curse of Allah be upon him) and Hamzah (may Allah be pleased with him). The intended meaning is general, as is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. Qatadah said: it was revealed informing about the state of the disbeliever and the believer in the Hereafter. So the disbelievers walk in it upon their faces, and the believers walk upright.

It is related that it was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "How does the disbeliever walk upon his face?" He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The One who made him walk on his feet in this world is able to make him walk on his face in the Hereafter."

Accordingly, there is no comparison. It has also been said that the intended meaning of mukibb is the blind person and of sawiyy is the one who sees. This is either by way of metonymy (kināyah) or by way of the sent metaphor (majāz mursal). It does not prevent taking it, after that, as a parable for those you have heard about, as is known in its proper place.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 23:

﴿Say: It is He who brought you into being and made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾ — i.e., the hearts (al-af'idah). ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾ — i.e., for those blessings, such as using your hearing to listen to the revealed verses (al-ayat al-tanziliyyah) so as to benefit from them, and your sight to look through them at the created signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah) that bear witness to the affairs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and your hearts to reflect, by means of them, on what you hear and see. ﴿Little﴾ is in the accusative because it is an adjective of an understood verbal noun (masdar muqaddar), i.e., "thanking a little," and "ma" is redundant (za'idah) for emphasizing the minimization. The clause is a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah). The smallness (qillah) is taken in its apparent sense, or in the sense of negation (nafy) if the address is to the disbelievers. It is also permissible for the clause to be a new, independent sentence (mustanifah), but the first (view) is preferable.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verses 24–25:

﴿He it is Who scattered you upon the earth﴾, i.e., created you and multiplied you therein, and none other than He, exalted and majestic is He; ﴿and unto Him you will be gathered﴾ for the recompense, not unto any other, glorified is He, whether in partnership or independently. ﴿Say, "Indeed, the knowledge"﴾ i.e., knowledge of its time ﴿is with Allah﴾, Mighty and Majestic, none other than Him, Mighty and Majestic, has access to it, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord."﴾ [al-A'raf: 187] ﴿And I am only a clear warner.﴾ I warn you of the occurrence of what has been promised, without doubt. The fa' in His saying ﴿فَلَمّا رَأوْهُ﴾ ("So when they see it") is an eloquent fa' (fa' fasihah), which indicates that two clauses have been omitted, and that the conditional clause is ordered after them. It is as if it were said: "The promised [punishment] has come to them, and they saw it, so when they saw it..." etc. This is similar to His saying ﴿فَلَمّا رَآهُ مُسْتَقِرًّا عِنْدَهُ﴾ ("So when he saw it settled in his presence") [An-Naml: 40], except that the omitted element there is an actual event, ordered after what precedes it by the fa', whereas here it is something treated as though it had occurred and introduced by way of resumption (istinaf).

His saying ﴿زُلْفَةً﴾ ("near") is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the object of ra'aw ("they saw"). It may be either: with an implied noun, meaning "possessing nearness and proximity"; or as a verbal noun in the sense of an active participle, meaning "drawing near"; or as a verbal noun used as an adjective for emphasis; or as an adverb of place, meaning "they saw it in a place of nearness." Some have explained zulfah as "near," and the matter is clear in this sense, as it is also according to what is reported from Ibn Zayd, that it means "present."

Al-Raghib said: "Zulfah means rank and favour. As for what is in the verse, it has been said that its meaning is 'the nearness of the believers,' and it has been said that it means 'nearness for them.' He used zulfah for the rank of punishment, just as bishārah ("glad tidings") and similar words have been used [in the opposite sense]." End of quote. There is no zulfah in either of these two views.

﴿سِيئَتْ وُجُوهُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed"): their faces were made evil by seeing it, in that they were overcome by gloom and dust and humiliation covered them. He placed the relative pronoun in the place of their pronoun, to censure them for disbelief and to make the evil of their state dependent upon it. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Shaybah, Ibn Thabbab, Talhah, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read the kasrah of sīʾat with ishmām (a faint pronunciation of the damma). (It has been said that) this is a rebuke to them and an intensification of punishment upon them.

﴿هَذا الَّذِي كُنْتُمْ بِهِ تَدَّعُونَ﴾ ("This is what you used to call for"): that is, what you used to seek in the world and hasten, as denial and mockery. On this reading, tadda'ūn is of the form tafta'ilūn from du'ā' (calling/praying for), and the bā' is a complement of the verb. It has also been said that it is from da'wā (claim), meaning "you claim that there is no resurrection and no gathering," in which case the bā' is causal, or indicates association with regard to the mention.

The first interpretation is supported by the reading of Abu Raja', al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Yasar, 'Abdullah ibn Muslim, Salam and Ya'qub, who read ﴿تَدَّعُونَ﴾ with a sukun on the dal. This is also the reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Abu Zayd, 'Ismah from Abu Bakr, and al-Asma'i from Nafi'. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in Surat al-Ma'arij that yad'ūn is a lightened form from their saying "da'ā bi-kadhā" when he demanded it. And it is reported from al-Farra' that it is from "da'awtu, ad'u" (I called). The meaning is: "This is what you used to seek hastily and call upon God to hasten it," referring to their saying ﴿إنْ كانَ هَذا هو الحَقَّ مِن عِنْدِكَ﴾ ("If this is indeed the truth from You") [Al-Anfal: 32], and so on.

It is reported from Mujahid that the promised thing was the punishment of the Day of Badr, and this is far-fetched. As for what has been said, that the promised thing was the sinking into the earth (khasf) and the hurling storm (hāṣib), and that both have occurred, because khasf here means humiliation, as in the verse of the poet:

"None dwells under a humiliation intended for him, except the two most abased: the donkey of the tribe and the tent-peg."

And by hāṣib is meant pebbles, and he (ﷺ) threw them in their faces, as in the well-known report. Or [it has been said that] neither occurred, based on what was first known about what is meant by them. That does not harm, since the threat being unfulfilled is not a defect. There is no problem in that. But this is nothing, as is not hidden.

The disbelievers of Makkah used to call down destruction upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and upon the believers. So Allah, glorified is He, said to him, peace and blessings be upon him:

Say: Have you considered?" That is, "Tell me," as is commonly held, and its analysis has already been discussed. "If God destroys me and those with me," that is, the believers, "or has mercy on us," that is, by granting us victory over you, "then who will protect the disbelievers from painful punishment?" That is, "then who will protect you from the punishment of the Fire?" The apparent noun has been used in place of the implied addressed pronoun, to indicate that the cause of perdition is certain. "So how" could they be granted protection? The apparent meaning is that the answer to the conditional and the thing it is joined to are one and the same. The overall meaning is: "There is no protector for you from the punishment of the Fire, because of your disbelief, which necessitates it. If we are returned to God's mercy through destruction, as you wish, then it contains the attainment of the bliss of the Hereafter, or through victory over you. The guidance for Islam is as we hope, because in that lies success in both of the desired goals." This also includes urging them to seek deliverance through faith, and that what they are engaged in is a preoccupation that distracts them from wishing for the destruction of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and those with him among the believers. This is the most preferred of three interpretations mentioned by al-Zamakhshari.

The second is that the meaning is: "If God destroys us by death, while we are your guides and those who hold fast to your reins, then who will protect you from the Fire? And if He has mercy on us by overcoming you and killing you, contrary to what you wish, then who will protect you, because the one killed at our hands is ruined in this world and the next." On this interpretation the answer is multiple, according to the multiplicity of its cause. He preferred the first interpretation, because it contains a rebuke of their opinion, since they seek what is the happiness of their enemies, and then an urging toward what is more fitting, which is deliverance from what they are in, namely the cause of destruction.

In this, the first is also present, insofar as they wish for the destruction of the one who would protect them from punishment by his guidance. The context also favours the first.

The third is that the meaning is: "If God destroys us in the Hereafter for our sins, while we are Muslims, then who will protect the disbelievers, who are more deserving of destruction because of their disbelief? And if He has mercy on us through faith, then who will protect one who has no faith?" On this interpretation the answer is also multiple. The destruction in it is understood figuratively rather than literally, as in the previous one. The purpose is to affirm definitively that they have no protector, and that their state, when it is caught between destruction by sin and mercy through faith, while they are believers, then what will be the state of one who has no faith? This carries a degree of remoteness.

﴿Say﴾: that is, as a reply to their wish for something that will not benefit them but will rather ruin them, alluding to the evil they are in. ﴿He is the Most Merciful﴾: that is, Allah, the Most Merciful. ﴿We have believed in Him﴾: that is, so that He will protect us by His mercy, Mighty and Majestic, from the punishment of the Hereafter, and we have not disbelieved as you have, so that we will not be recompensed at all. Since He made disbelief the cause of evil in the first verse, He made belief the cause of protection in this one, so that the antithesis (tuqābul) is complete and the allusion (taʿrīḍ) falls in its proper place. He did not place the object before "āmannā" because if it had been said "bihi āmannā," it would have turned toward an allusion to their belief in idols, and would have departed from what the speech was directed at.

The fronting in His words, "and upon Him we have relied" (وعليه توكلنا), is excellent because the allusion to them concerns the matter of reliance. That is: "and upon Him we have relied, and excellent is the Trustee." Our victory is not by numbers and equipment, as yours is. The summary is this: since He mentioned earlier destruction and mercy, and explained mercy as the mercy of this world and the Hereafter, He here affirmed that they attain it in both abodes, because of their belief and their reliance upon Him alone. In this is confirmation that it is not attained by the disbelievers, due to the absence of its causes. Then the verse has a conclusion in the manner of the preceding verses, and a clarification that the best deed is belief and trust in Allah alone, and that this is the reality of piety. His words, ﴿So you will know who is in clear error﴾: that is, in both abodes. It is a threat after summarizing the cause, but it was delivered in the form of fair speech, meaning: who among us and you is in error, etc. Al-Kisāʾī read "fasayaʿlamūna" with the ya of the third person, considering His words ﴿Who will protect the disbelievers?﴾

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 67, verse 30:

His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Say: Have you considered?﴾ That is, tell me. ﴿If your water should become sunken (ghawran)﴾ That is, sunk (ghair), gone away into the earth entirely. It is also reported from al-Kalbi that it means it cannot be reached by buckets. It is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a description for emphasis, or it is interpreted as an active participle (ism al-fa'il).

Whatever the case, the intended meaning of "water" is not flowing water, even though the verse, as Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Fakihi reported from Ibn al-Kalbi, was revealed concerning the well of Zamzam and the well of Maymun ibn al-Hadrami: ﴿then who will bring you flowing water?﴾ That is, running water, or apparent water, easy to obtain, since hands can reach it. It is either fa'il from ma'an (to flow), or maf'ul from ma'an (to be made available). This is a threat in this world only.

The previous threat was followed by this one as a reminder, by means of the lesser to the greater: if you do not worship Him, mighty and majestic, for the everlasting life, then worship Him for the transient one. This verse was recited in the presence of some of the mockers, and when he heard ﴿who will bring you﴾ and so on, he said: "Axes and hoes will bring it," and the water of his eyes went away (i.e., he went blind).

We seek refuge in Allah, exalted, from audacity toward Allah, majestic in His majesty, and toward His verses. Interpreting the verses in this manner is what some of the imams chose, but it is further from the intended meaning than others, and Allah, exalted, knows best the secrets of His speech.
